Illinois as part of New Meridian Testing in 2021
• As you are all aware, the pandemic made for a complicated year of
testing.
• Accountability waivers were granted for states but testing waivers were
not universally granted.
• The New Meridian consortium was broadly impacted by testing
changes:
• DC was given a waiver to not test in 2021.
• NJ tested using an abbreviated form (Start Strong) in Fall 2021
• IL tested in spring 2021 and offered Fall 2021 testing
• BIE and DoDEA testing in spring 2021.
• States that tested did not see test participation at levels normally
observed (i.e., 95%).
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

SGP Operational Considerations in 2021
• Illinois (and New Meridian) growth analyses are skip-year/gap year growth from 2019 to
• In prior years, only cohort referenced (SIMEX and non-measurement error corrected)
SGPs were calculated.
• In 2021, four types of SGP analyses were conducted for Illinois (and New Meridian) data:
• Cohort referenced analyses: These analyses create growth norms from the 2019 to 2021
students. These growth norms yield cohort means/median SGPs of 50 and obscure COVID-19
academic impact. Both SIMEX (measurement error corrected) and non-SIMEX SGPs are
calculated.
• Baseline referenced analyses: Historical growth norms were created using 2019 and prior data.
These growth growth analyses don’t have mean/median SGPs of 50 and can be used to
investigate overall COVID-19 academic impact. Both SIMEX (measurement error corrected) and
non-SIMEX SGPs are calculated.
• Projections (lagged and straight) were calculated for 2021 data using baseline growth
norms in case they were needed.
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

SGP Summary of Cohort versus Baseline Referenced
• Cohort referenced SGPs
• Growth norms created from the current cohort of students.
• Typical way that SGPs are calculated.
• Both consortium and state referenced norms are created.
• Mean/median will by 50 for all grade x content area analyses.
• Cannot investigate overall impact of the pandemic on students.
• Can investigate differential impact of the pandemic on students.
• Does not require scale stability across years.
• Baseline referenced SGPs.
• Growth norms created from historical (i.e., pre-COVID) cohorts of students.
• Mean/median 50 for historical cohort, not necessarily 50 for current cohort.
• Both consortium and state referenced baseline norms are created (using 2019 membership)
• Extent of deviation from (i.e. below) 50 is indicative of less learning/pandemic related academic impact.
• Mean SGP deviation of 5 corresponds to an effect size of 0.18.
• Can investigate BOTH overall impact and differential impact
• Requires scale stability across years.
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

SGP Calculations
• SGP calculations were performed using the SGP package and R software
environment based upon data supplied by Pearson.
• To facilitate the calculation of baseline SGPs across multiple states, we
created an additional R package, SGPmatrices, that contains all baseline
matrices for states/organizations.
• SGPmatrices
• Source code associated with calculations are available on GitHub (private
account):
• Illinois GitHub Repo
• Analyses were conducted first by state/organization based upon availability
of data provided by Pearson and then at the consortium level once all data
was available.

SGP Assumptions
• SGP analyses presume valid scale scores
• Students forming the growth norm group are presumed to have taken
the same (or equivalent) test at the same time. Scores have to mean the
same thing.
• SGPs, however, are often used as a post-hoc check of scale score
validity/comparability via Reductio ad absurdum
• In 2021, check form comparability and mode-of-administration
comparability.
• Illinois has experience (e.g., PARCC paper/pencil versus online)
investigating and accommodating mode-effects.
• If scores are not comparable then we either attempt to make them
comparable or run separate analyses.

SGP Analyses and Academic Impact
• Understanding pandemic related impact necessarily requires looking back to
pre-pandemic results.
• The impulse of stakeholders to want to compare 2021 results with 2019
results is the correct impulse at both the individual, school, district, and state
level.
• Wanting to look at 2019 to 2021 change is an attempt to investigate impact.
• The challenge is making 2019 to 2021 comparisons apples-to-apples
comparisons.
• Supporting these comparisons requires having a complete understanding is
who constitutes the missing data.
• IL provided additional data in September 2021 indicating which students were
missing.

Points of Clarification for Status Results
• Decrease in attainment (as a decrease in percent proficient) between
2019 and 2021 is the most often reported statistic related to state testing
in 2021.
• This analysis & statistic (percent proficient) are problematic for several
reasons:
• Using 2019 as a counterfactual for where students would have been had
the pandemic not occurred is problematic for several reasons including:
• Changes in student cohort composition is not accounted for.
• Improvement between 2019 and 2021 that would have occurred is not
accounted for.
• Missing data in 2021 not accounted for.
• Multiple imputation results imply results would have been lower had all students
tested.
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Points of Clarification for Status Results

• Effect sizes associated with decreases range from approximately 0.15 to 0.4.
• Participation rates (derived from decreases in observed test scores between
2019 and 2021) vary by grade and state/organization but suggest
participation between 60% and 80% (mostly toward the lower end)
• In general, the achievement decreases observed are large and are consistent
with large academic impact.
• Other states, with and without missing data, show similar decreases.
• In general, current results based upon incomplete data likely represent a best-
case scenario compared to what would appear given fuller participation.

Discussion
• Median baseline SGPs in ELA and Math were in the mid to low 30s.
• Deviation from normal growth (i.e., 50) represents the extent to which academic
growth slowed down from 2019 to 2021, that is, academic impact.
• Comparably large academic impact in ELA than mathematics.
• Comparably large academic impact across grades.
• Given what we know about student growth, academic impact will likely require
multiple years and additional educational supports/interventions to recover.
• To have average progress (i.e., SGP = 50) over a time span, deviations below 50 must be
compensated with commensurate deviations above 50.
• For example, a 2 year median SGP of 35 would need to be followed by a 2 year median SGP
of 65 to ”average out” at 50.

Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Discussion of Ethnicity Results
• Broken out by ethnicity, 2021 baseline SGP results show similar
rank ordering (i.e., growth gaps) as seen in normal years.
• Student academic growth is comparable in mathematics and ELA
for all ethnic subgroups.
• Growth decreases by ethnicity are relatively uniform across
different ethnic groups.

Participation Rates and Interpretation
• An issue impacting the interpretation of growth (and status) results in
2021 is participation in the state assessment.
• Low participation doesn’t impact calculation of cohort referenced
growth norms nor use of baseline referenced growth norms.
• Low participation does impact comparisons of group level results with
historical (e.g., 2019) results based upon higher participation rates.
• For example, how should one compare growth and status results for
school in 2019 and 2021 with very different rates of participation.

Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Multiple Imputation
• Given the rich historical data available for students missing in 2021,
and the observed performance of comparable students from 2019
to 2021, it is possible to simulate what we think their performance
might have been.
• Combining multiple simulations can inform us about potential bias
in what we observed at state/district/school levels in 2021, as well
as inform us about levels of uncertainty around them.
• Multiple imputation (MI) of missing data is widely adopted and
well-developed statistical analysis technique used in many fields to
deal with missing data problems.

Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Multiple Imputation
• MI uses information from the observed data to generate
parameter estimates in three steps:
• Imputation: A prediction model generates a set of plausible values
for the missing observations, resulting in M imputed data sets.
• Analysis: The analysis (e.g., baseline student growth percentiles) is
conducted on each of the M data sets.
• Pooling: Parameter and (more importantly) uncertainty estimates
are constructed by pooling across the M analyses.

Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Multiple Imputation
• In the context of COVID impact analyses, we use the multiple
(plausible) parameter estimates to inform us about the
uncertainty around what was observed. That is, we do not use
MI to produce “corrected” parameter estimates, but rather to
help determine whether we trust the statistics calculated from
the observed (with missing) data.
• Statistics of particular interest:
• Mean/median scale scores
• Mean/median baseline SGPs
• Effect size estimates
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Multiple Imputation
• Before performing a MI analysis with Illinois (and New Meridian
data in general) data, missing data patterns were investigated.
• Patterns suggest some relationship to factors such as prior
achievement and economic status.
• These relationships suggest that missing data in Illinois is non-
ignorable, but does not preclude the use of MI.
• Data can be considered “Missing-at-random” – relationships exist between
missingness and the observed data (and so can not be considered “missing
completely-at-random”) but the relationships are not systematic (e.g. all
students below proficiency in 2019 were missing in 2021).

Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

District & School Level Results
• Due to larger fluctuations in participation rates at the district and school level,
growth comparisons between 2019 and 2021 must be approached more
cautiously.
• In general, in other states we have had good success via multiple imputation
that comparisons of status and growth results from 2019 to 2021.
• Multiple imputation indicates both when inference is defensible based upon
observed data and when such an inference appears problematic.
• We have found that whether a school’s results support cross-year comparison
depends more on the size of the school than on the participation rate/
enrollment change.

Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

SGP Analysis Plans post 2021 (2022 and beyond)
• Spring 2021 represented an ideal time to get a snapshot of student attainment as
we are presumably/hopefully at or near the point of maximal impact on student
attainment.
• That is, recovery had not really begun for most students in earnest.
• It’s impossible to talk about recovery sensibly without understanding how big the
impact is.
• Analytics in 2022 will be keenly interested on whether or not recovery is
occurring: Who, what, how much.
• Monitoring recovery will be at least as critical as monitoring the impact of the
pandemic on student achievement.
• Beware the K-shaped recovery!
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Communication of Results in 2021
• Technical challenges to the calculation of growth in 2021 are likely
minor compared to communication challenges.
• State reporting is, in general, highly aligned with accountability.
• Even though analyses outlined herein deal with status/growth, they
don’t necessarily align with accountability narratives.
• It is critical for leadership (at the highest level) to map out a
communication plan and then build analytics and reporting to support
that plan.
• Without a well considered, disciplined and coordinated communication
plan, accountability narratives are likely to take over.
Illinois TAC 12/2/2021

Summary of Findings
• SGP analyses were successfully conducted for Illinois members testing
in spring 2021 and fall 2021
• Results of the analyses suggest large academic impacts on students due
to the pandemic.
• Results are large in both math and in ELA. Results were large in both
elementary and middle school grades.
• Results show variation across academic subgroups (e.g., high versus low
achievers in some content areas).
• Recovery from impacts this large will likely take multiple years and
require additional supports beyond that provided by normal schooling.
